ta-l1d1q3-d1e3501.summary: Opens the question on what is to be used, asking whether everything other than God is to be used. The first objection says no. To use is to take something into the faculty of the will, which applies only to what falls under our operation, and not all creatures do: the heavens and the angels cannot be worked upon by us.
claims: Only what is subject to our operation can be taken into the faculty of the will.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3504.summary: Second objection. We use what helps us toward beatitude, but creatures often hinder us. Wisdom 14:11 says creatures became an abomination, a temptation to souls, and a snare for the feet of the foolish. So not everything can be used.
claims: Creatures frequently impede rather than assist progress toward beatitude.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3510.summary: Third objection. If we must use everything other than God, then whenever we fail to refer something to God we sin, and whenever we refer it we merit. Every act would then be either meritorious or sinful, and none would be indifferent.
claims: If all things must be referred to God, there are no morally indifferent acts.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3514.summary: Fourth objection. It would follow that no sin is venial. If an act is referred to the ultimate end it is no sin, and if some other end is set up as ultimate and not referred to God it is mortal sin. Since every rational act is for some end, there is no room for venial sin.
claims: If every end is either the ultimate end or set up against it, there is no venial sin.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3517.summary: Sed contra from 1 Corinthians 10:31: whether you eat or drink, do all things for the glory of God. So everything is to be used.
claims: Scripture commands that all things be done for the glory of God.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3528.summary: Second sed contra. God is perfect in goodness as he is perfect in power. It belongs to the perfection of his power that nothing exists unless produced by him, so it belongs to the perfection of his goodness that nothing be loved except in ordering to him.
claims: The perfection of divine goodness requires that nothing be loved except in ordering to God, as the perfection of divine power requires that nothing exist except from God.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3531.summary: Thomas's determination. All goods are good only by approaching likeness to divine goodness, and goodness is the ground of love, so everything must be loved in ordering to the first goodness. What is not from God is neither to be sought nor used, so sin, which is not from God, is never to be used. Punishment is from God and is to be used for the end: it advances merit by bringing a person to consider their weakness, and it purges sin. Worldly things are from God and are to be used either as leading to knowledge of him, by showing his greatness, or as supporting a life ordered to God. Our good works are to be done for God's sake. Not every operation must be actually referred to God; it suffices that the will has habitually set its end in God.
claims: Everything good is to be loved in ordering to the first goodness.
Sin is never to be used, but punishment is to be used, since it is from God and promotes merit and purgation.
Habitual, not actual, reference of operations to God suffices.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3534.summary: Reply to the first objection. We use creatures such as the heavens and the angels not as things we work upon but as things that lead us to knowledge of God.
claims: Creatures beyond human operation are used insofar as they lead to the knowledge of God.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3537.summary: Reply to the second objection. Creatures in themselves do not hinder us from attaining beatitude. The hindrance comes from our side, when we abuse them by resting in them as if in an end.
claims: Creatures hinder beatitude only through our abuse of them, when we treat them as ends.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3541.summary: Reply to the third objection. For the theologian, no act proceeding from deliberate will is indifferent. If it is referred to God, given grace, it is meritorious; if it cannot be referred, it is a sin; if it can be referred but is not, it is vain, and idleness counts among sins for the theologian.
claims: No deliberate act is morally indifferent for the theologian.
An act referable to God but not referred is vain, and idleness is a sin.

ta-l1d1q3-d1e3544.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Someone who sins venially does not actually refer their act to God, yet still has God habitually as their end. They do not make the creature their ultimate end, since they love it short of God; they sin by excess in love, like someone who lingers too long on the road without leaving it.
claims: Venial sin consists in excessive love of a creature that remains habitually ordered to God, not in making it an ultimate end.

ta-l1d1q3-Dd1e3493.summary: Article 1 (the only article) asks whether everything other than God is to be used. Objections appeal to creatures beyond human operation, to creatures as snares, and to the apparent consequences that no act would be indifferent and no sin venial. The sed contra cites 1 Cor. 10:31 and the parallel between divine power and divine goodness. Thomas holds that every good is to be loved in ordering to the first goodness. Sin, not being from God, is never to be used; punishment, worldly things, and good works, being from God, are to be used. Habitual rather than actual reference to God suffices. The replies explain the use of creatures as leading to knowledge of God and locate their harm in our abuse. They deny that any deliberate act is indifferent for the theologian and explain venial sin as excessive love that stays within a habitual ordering to God.
claims: Everything good other than God is to be used, i.e. loved in ordering to God; sin is never to be used.
Habitual ordering to God suffices for right use.
No deliberate act is indifferent; venial sin is excess within an ordering to God.

ta-l1d1q3.summary: Quaestio 3 of Book I, Distinction 1 treats the objects of use, asking in a single article whether everything other than God is to be used. Thomas grounds the universality of use in participation: every created good is good by likeness to the divine goodness and must be loved in ordering to it. He refines this by excluding sin (not from God) and including punishment, created things, and good works, and by requiring only habitual, not actual, reference to God. This yields the theological thesis that no deliberate act is morally indifferent, together with an account of venial sin as disordered excess that does not abandon God as end.
claims: All goods other than God are to be used in ordering to God, since they are good by participating in divine goodness.
No deliberate act is morally indifferent; venial sin remains within a habitual ordering to God.
